questions.stem: A 6-year-old with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is going home between chemotherapy cycles. The absolute neutrophil count is 400/mm3. The younger sibling is due for the MMR and varicella vaccines. Which instruction should the nurse give the parents?

options.text: Call right away for a temperature of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher
Delay the sibling's MMR and varicella vaccines until chemotherapy ends
Check a rectal temperature if the child feels warm
Give acetaminophen for a fever and call if it lasts 24 hours

rationale.correct: Neutropenia: report fever of 38 °C or higher right away, no rectal temperatures, no live vaccines for the child; household contacts should be vaccinated.

perOption.a: Fever with neutropenia can mean sepsis and needs same-hour evaluation and antibiotics.
perOption.b: Household contacts should receive MMR and varicella; spread of these vaccine viruses is rare.
perOption.c: Rectal temperatures risk mucosal injury and infection.
perOption.d: Fever in neutropenia is an emergency, and acetaminophen can hide it.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach infection precautions for a child with leukemia.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease and a cold for 2 days suddenly becomes pale, limp and fussy. The heart rate is 170/min, the blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg and the spleen is felt 6 cm below the left ribs. Yesterday it could not be felt. Hemoglobin has fallen from 8.2 to 4.1 g/dL. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Splenic sequestration crisis
Vaso-occlusive pain crisis
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19
Acute chest syndrome

rationale.correct: Splenic sequestration: pallor, an enlarging spleen and hypovolemic shock; transfusion is needed.

perOption.a: Blood pools in the spleen, causing a rapid fall in hemoglobin and shock; this is an emergency.
perOption.b: This causes pain, not an enlarging spleen with shock.
perOption.c: This lowers hemoglobin over days, without a sudden large spleen.
perOption.d: This causes chest pain, fever and hypoxia with lung infiltrates.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with moderate hemophilia A wants to join an after-school sport with friends. The child has had two knee bleeds this year and receives factor VIII prophylaxis at home three times a week. Which activity should the nurse suggest as the safest choice?

options.text: Swimming
Basketball
Ice hockey
Soccer

rationale.correct: Hemophilia: encourage non-contact activity; teach factor replacement and joint protection.

perOption.a: Non-contact sports reduce the risk of joint and muscle bleeds.
perOption.b: Jumping and contact raise the risk of joint bleeds.
perOption.c: This is a high-contact sport.
perOption.d: Kicking and collisions risk knee and ankle bleeds.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old drinks about 1.4 L (48 oz) of whole cow's milk a day, eats little solid food and is pale and irritable. The child's weight is at the 75th percentile. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Iron deficiency anemia
Lead poisoning from the home
Vitamin D deficiency rickets
Hypercalcemia from milk intake

rationale.correct: Limit milk to about 470 to 710 mL (16 to 24 oz) a day for toddlers and offer iron-rich foods.

perOption.a: Too much milk displaces iron-rich foods and can cause small amounts of GI blood loss.
perOption.b: This causes anemia, but the history points to milk intake.
perOption.c: Milk is fortified with vitamin D, so this is unlikely.
perOption.d: This is not a typical result of milk intake.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize risk for iron deficiency in toddlers.

questions.stem: A parent rushes in carrying a 2-year-old who may have swallowed several of a grandparent's pills about 30 minutes ago. The pill bottle is not with them. The child is drowsy, the respiratory rate is 8/min and the SpO2 is 86%. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Open the airway and support breathing with a bag-valve mask
Give activated charcoal by mouth to bind the pills
Ask the parent to call the grandparent to name the pills
Draw blood for a toxicology screen and acetaminophen level

rationale.correct: Poisoning: ABCs, identify the substance, contact poison control and give specific treatment.

perOption.a: Slow breathing and low SpO2 threaten life; the airway and breathing come first.
perOption.b: Charcoal is unsafe in a drowsy child without a protected airway.
perOption.c: Identifying the drug matters, but it does not come before breathing.
perOption.d: Labs follow stabilization.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care in a suspected poisoning.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old swallowed a mouthful of liquid drain cleaner 10 minutes ago. The child is drooling and crying and has red patches on the lips. The parent asks whether to give syrup to make the child throw up. Which action should the nurse avoid?

options.text: Inducing vomiting
Assessing the airway for stridor and swelling
Contacting the poison control center
Looking in the mouth for burns

rationale.correct: Caustic ingestion: no induced vomiting and no neutralizing agents; watch for airway swelling and prepare for endoscopy.

perOption.a: Vomiting re-exposes the esophagus and airway to the caustic substance.
perOption.b: Airway swelling can develop quickly and must be watched.
perOption.c: Poison control guides management.
perOption.d: This helps judge the extent of injury.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent calls the clinic because a 3-year-old may have swallowed a coin-sized button battery from a remote control about an hour ago. The child is eating, playing and has no symptoms. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Go to the emergency department now for an x-ray
Watch the stools for the battery over the next few days
Give a laxative to help the battery pass more quickly
Bring the child in if pain, drooling or vomiting starts

rationale.correct: Button battery ingestion is an emergency that may need urgent endoscopic removal; honey may be given on the way per poison control.

perOption.a: Button batteries in the esophagus can burn through the tissue within 2 hours, even without symptoms.
perOption.b: Waiting can allow a serious esophageal burn.
perOption.c: This does not address a battery lodged in the esophagus.
perOption.d: Severe injury can occur before symptoms appear.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the urgency of button battery ingestion.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old living in a house built in 1950 has a blood lead level of 50 mcg/dL and is admitted to start chelation therapy with succimer. Which intervention is most important during chelation?

options.text: Encourage fluids and monitor kidney function
Restrict fluids to concentrate the lead in the urine
Stop the therapy if the urine output increases
Give a multivitamin with iron with each succimer dose

rationale.correct: Lead poisoning: remove the source, chelation as needed and monitor the kidneys.

perOption.a: Chelated lead is excreted in the urine and can stress the kidneys.
perOption.b: This increases the risk of kidney injury.
perOption.c: Increased urine output is acceptable.
perOption.d: Iron is not given with succimer.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old is admitted with dehydration and chickenpox. New spots appeared this morning, and the child has been afebrile for 24 hours. The parent asks when isolation can stop. What is the nurse's response?

options.text: "When the last of the spots have crusted over."
"Now, because the fever has been gone for a full day."
"After 24 hours of IV acyclovir treatment."
"Once no new spots have appeared for 12 hours."

rationale.correct: Varicella: airborne and contact precautions until all lesions crust; avoid contact with pregnant or immunocompromised people.

perOption.a: Varicella is contagious until all lesions are crusted.
perOption.b: The child may still be contagious after the fever ends.
perOption.c: Acyclovir does not end contagiousness.
perOption.d: Existing lesions must crust over.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 4-year-old is diagnosed with rubella. The family lives with an aunt who is 10 weeks pregnant, a grandparent with high blood pressure and a vaccinated 8-year-old sibling. Who is most important for the child to avoid?

options.text: The aunt who is 10 weeks pregnant
The grandparent with high blood pressure
The vaccinated 8-year-old sibling
Other children at the same daycare

rationale.correct: Rubella's main danger is to the fetus; vaccination prevents it.

perOption.a: Rubella in early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome.
perOption.b: Rubella is usually mild in adults.
perOption.c: The sibling is immune.
perOption.d: They need notice, but the fetus is at greatest risk.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A pediatric clinic sees four children with fever and a rash on the same day. The nurse reviews each child's history and exam so that the right isolation precautions can be started and families can be told who else may be at risk. For each childhood illness, indicate its characteristic finding.

columns.text: Vesicles in different stages at the same time
Small white spots on the inside of the cheeks
High fever for 3 days, then a rash as the fever breaks

rationale.correct: Know the hallmark findings of common childhood rashes.

perOption.r1:c1: Crops of lesions in different stages are typical.
perOption.r1:c2: These are Koplik spots of measles.
perOption.r2:c2: Koplik spots appear before the measles rash.
perOption.r3:c3: The slapped-cheek rash is typical of parvovirus B19.
perOption.r4:c4: The rash appears as the high fever ends.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has intense itching that is worse at night and thin, wavy burrows between the fingers. Scabies is diagnosed. The child lives with two parents and a baby sibling with no symptoms. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Treat everyone in the home with permethrin on the same day
Treat the child now, and the others if they start to itch
Expect the itching to stop within a day of the first treatment
Air the bedding outside in the sun for an afternoon

rationale.correct: Scabies: treat all contacts, wash linens in hot water or bag them for 72 hours or more.

perOption.a: Contacts may be infested before symptoms appear; treating together prevents reinfestation.
perOption.b: Others may be infested without symptoms yet.
perOption.c: Itching can last 2 to 4 weeks after successful treatment.
perOption.d: Linens are washed in hot water or bagged for 72 hours.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A school nurse has taught the parent of an 8-year-old with head lice about treatment and preventing spread to the other children in the family. Which statement by the parent needs correction?

options.text: "I'll comb out the nits with a fine-tooth comb each day."
"I'll wash the pillowcases and hats in hot water."
"It's fine for the kids to keep sharing hairbrushes."
"I'll check everyone else's hair for lice tonight."

rationale.correct: Lice: pediculicide, nit removal, washing items and no sharing of hair items.

perOption.a: This removes the eggs.
perOption.b: This kills lice on items.
perOption.c: Sharing hair items spreads lice.
perOption.d: Checking household members is appropriate.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old who attends daycare has red sores around the nose and mouth that started as small blisters 3 days ago and now have honey-colored crusts. The child has no fever. What should the nurse teach the parent?

options.text: The sores are contagious, so wash hands and use separate towels
The rash is eczema, so a moisturizing cream will clear it
The child has fifth disease and can return to daycare now
The sores are cold sores, which will heal on their own

rationale.correct: Impetigo: topical or oral antibiotics, hygiene, short nails and return to daycare 24 hours after starting antibiotics.

perOption.a: Impetigo is a contagious bacterial skin infection.
perOption.b: Honey-colored crusts suggest impetigo, not eczema.
perOption.c: Fifth disease causes a slapped-cheek rash.
perOption.d: Cold sores are grouped vesicles, not honey-colored crusts.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with a positive rapid strep test is prescribed amoxicillin for 10 days. The parent says the child usually feels better in a couple of days. Which statement by the parent shows understanding?

options.text: "My child will finish all 10 days, even if feeling better."
"I'll stop it once the fever and sore throat are gone."
"I'll save the extra doses for the next sore throat."
"My child stays home from school for the full 10 days."

rationale.correct: Complete strep treatment to prevent rheumatic fever.

perOption.a: Completing the course prevents complications like rheumatic fever.
perOption.b: Stopping early risks rheumatic fever.
perOption.c: Saving antibiotics leads to incomplete treatment.
perOption.d: Children can return after 12 to 24 hours of antibiotics and no fever.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach adherence to strep throat treatment.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing four children in the emergency department. Which finding most strongly suggests physical abuse?

options.text: A spiral femur fracture in a 4-month-old who cannot roll over
Bruises of different colors on the shins of an active 4-year-old
A buckle fracture of the wrist in a 7-year-old who fell off a bike
A bump on the forehead of a 13-month-old learning to walk

rationale.correct: Red flags: injuries that do not fit the child's development or the history, patterned injuries and delays in seeking care.

perOption.a: A twisting fracture in an infant who cannot move independently does not fit the child's development.
perOption.b: Shin bruises in different stages are common in active children.
perOption.c: A fall on an outstretched hand commonly causes this fracture.
perOption.d: Forehead bumps are common in new walkers.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old is brought in by a parent's partner for lethargy, vomiting and poor feeding since last night. The partner says the baby "was fine" and denies any fall. The fontanel is full, and an eye exam shows bleeding in both retinas. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome)
Viral gastroenteritis with dehydration
Bacterial meningitis
Retinal bleeding left from the birth

rationale.correct: Abusive head trauma: lethargy, vomiting, seizures, retinal hemorrhages; report as required.

perOption.a: Retinal hemorrhages with these signs and no history of injury strongly suggest abusive head trauma.
perOption.b: This does not cause retinal hemorrhages or a full fontanel.
perOption.c: This can cause a full fontanel but not retinal hemorrhages.
perOption.d: Birth-related retinal bleeding clears by about 4 to 6 weeks.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old has dropped from the 50th to below the 3rd percentile for weight. The infant avoids eye contact, has a severe diaper rash and gains weight quickly in the hospital on a normal diet. No medical cause is found. What may these findings suggest?

options.text: Neglect with failure to thrive
A small infant following a normal growth pattern
A milk protein allergy causing malabsorption
Normal shyness for the infant's age

rationale.correct: Assess feeding, the environment and the parent-child relationship; report suspected neglect.

perOption.a: Poor growth that improves with feeding in hospital, without a medical cause, suggests neglect.
perOption.b: A drop across several percentiles needs evaluation.
perOption.c: Weight gain on a normal diet argues against this.
perOption.d: Avoiding eye contact with poor growth is a warning sign.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching home safety to the parent of an 18-month-old who has started climbing on furniture. Which statement by the parent shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I keep medicines and cleaners in a locked cabinet."
"I leave my toddler in the tub for a minute to grab a towel."
"I've put covers on the outlets the toddler can reach."
"I've installed gates at the top and bottom of the stairs."

rationale.correct: Toddler safety: constant supervision near water, poison storage, gates and car seats.

perOption.a: This prevents poisoning.
perOption.b: Toddlers can drown in seconds in very little water.
perOption.c: This prevents electrical injury.
perOption.d: This prevents falls.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The school nurse is planning an injury-prevention program for a high school. Which cause of injury death among adolescents should the program focus on first?

options.text: Motor vehicle crashes
Choking on food
Poisoning from household products
Falls from playground equipment

rationale.correct: Teen safety: seat belts, no texting while driving, avoid impaired driving and use graduated licensing.

perOption.a: Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death in teens.
perOption.b: This is more common in young children.
perOption.c: This is more common in toddlers.
perOption.d: This is more common in young children.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old who recently moved from another country is brought in for crying and refusing to bear weight on the legs. The hands and feet are swollen, warm and tender, and the temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F). The infant has not had a newborn screen. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Dactylitis from sickle cell disease
An allergic reaction to a new food
Fractures from a fall or rough handling
Kawasaki disease after a viral infection

rationale.correct: Dactylitis is an early vaso-occlusive event; treat with fluids and pain relief.

perOption.a: Hand-foot syndrome is often the first sign of sickle cell disease in infants.
perOption.b: Allergy causes hives or swelling, not warm, tender hands and feet with fever.
perOption.c: Symmetric swelling of both hands and feet is not typical of fractures.
perOption.d: Kawasaki causes swelling but needs 5 days of fever with red eyes and lips.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize dactylitis in sickle cell disease.
